summary: Beneath Knurów, a coal-mining town in southern Poland where a team member’s grandfather worked in the mines, the ground is quietly sinking. Using NISAR’s L-band radar interferometry, we measured parts of the town dropping up to 39 cm in just four months of summer 2026, and a 1933 map reveals one point has sunk about 9 metres since. Changes like these are hard to see from the ground, and the data that exposes them is hard for non-specialists to read. Through NISAR's Lens makes it accessible. Our interactive web application’s Explorer combines scientific products from multiple sources, animates surface changes as a time series and links directly to full-resolution data. It also features a 3D satellite model users can take apart, illustrations of how microwaves interact with different surfaces, a guide to reading SAR imagery and live orbit tracking. Because NISAR reveals change while it is happening, not decades later, it can flag sinking ground, saturated soil and shifting dams before they turn into disasters. Our project puts that early warning in the hands of residents, planners and educators wherever Earth’s surface is changing.
details:
What it does

Through NISAR's Lens turns NISAR's radar data into something anyone can explore. Pick a place in the Explorer and see how its surface has changed. Turn the satellite around in 3D and learn what each part does. Read a plain-language guide to radar interferometry, and follow NISAR's live orbit.

Proof: Knurów, Poland

One of our team members' grandfathers worked in the coal mines of Knurów, a mining town in Silesia. Since the 1933 map was drawn, the town has sunk about 18m, and in summer 2026 the ground dropped 39 cm in four months. Satellite radar can flag changes like this while they are happening, not decades later.

Intended impact
  • Students and teachers: an interactive way to learn how Earth's surface changes and how we measure it from space.
  • People in at-risk areas: a view of what's happening under their own streets.
  • Curious minds of any age: real NASA science, no remote-sensing degree needed.
Artistic touch

Our graphic designer drew every illustration and edited every photo, giving the project its own look instead of stock images. Our typography echoes NASA's logo lettering to bring a sense of space exploration.

Tools
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no build step
  • Three.js (0.160): the 3D model you can take apart, the globe and the live orbit
  • CesiumJS (1.146): the 3D globe
  • D3-geo and TopoJSON: map projections
  • Esri Dark Gray Canvas and hillshade basemaps, OpenStreetMap tiles and Nominatim place search in the Explorer
  • Google Fonts: Krona One, Nasalisation
  • GitHub Pages: hosting
  • SI: Claude
